title: Why Do Students Hate Homework? (And How Can We Help Them to See It Can Help!) -help-them-to-see-it-can-help/
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino opens with a composite portrait of 'Harriet', a Year 11 student overwhelmed by exam-paper homework across every subject and demoralised by detentions for falling short of online quiz thresholds, to illustrate why so many students come to resent homework even when the underlying intention is sound. She lists the concrete complaints students raise -- excessive volume, busywork with no perceived value, lack of consistent feedback, and unrecognised effort -- alongside evidence that homework's mental-health costs and shaky research base have prompted policy responses like California's Healthy Homework Act. Castelino's own view is that purposeful practice does support fluency, but that too much practice without support, understanding, or feedback erodes any benefit through stress and apathy. Her proposed fixes operate at the whole-school level first: a clear, shared understanding of what homework is meant to achieve, protected staff time to design and evaluate it, sensible limits on total workload across subjects (potentially through centralising homework design), and -- most importantly -- homework that adapts to what a given student has already mastered rather than one-size-fits-all worksheets.
points: Castelino's 'Harriet' composite makes an abstract policy problem concrete: a student who wants to succeed is punished by a homework system that conflates volume with rigour, producing resentment rather than learning.

Her list of student-reported complaints (busywork, no feedback, unrecognised effort, unrealistic volume) functions as an evidence base drawn from real student experience, not just theoretical critique of homework as a concept.

The framing that purposeful practice supports fluency, but excessive unsupported practice erodes it through stress, gives a precise dose-response model for homework rather than a blanket 'homework good/bad' stance.

Her proposal to centralise homework design so it can be pre-planned and adaptable -- freeing staff time for feedback rather than task creation -- reframes the homework problem as a workload-allocation problem at the school-leadership level, not just a classroom-level teacher choice.
quotes: Harriet used to love talking about what she learnt at school. She would come home and tell her Mum all about the different states of matter, rivers, and her times tables.
On first glance, it might seem that homework killed Harriet's enthusiasm for learning.
The homework set seems to be busywork- students don't see the value in completing it.
The Healthy Homework Act recently took effect in California with the primary goal to promote evidence-based homework practices to support student learning and well-being.

We know that more purposeful practice can help towards fluency. But too much practice or practice with no support, understanding or feedback can lead to the benefits being diminished by stress, pressure and apathy.
Without these, no matter how much research you read or how much you say the right things about homework, the right culture is not cultivated.
But adaptable homework is far more powerful than pre-planned homework, especially if the latter builds on content over time.
